passage:
Sunday was room-cleaning day in the flats on Mango Lane, and three doors opened onto three messes.

Sahil stood in the middle of his and felt his chest tighten. Too much. Then he said aloud, "Clothes first." Next came books, then toys, then the floor. With each part done, the room looked a little smaller.

Shalini scooped everything off her floor and dumped it on the bed. It made one big heap, and she could finally see what she owned. Piles grew: cupboard, shelf, and the bin bag.

Vishal heard his mother's footsteps and shoved clutter under the bed. The floor shone. On Monday morning he lay on his stomach hunting for his school shoes, and behind the bed skirt he saw the mess exactly as it had been.

The chore that kept piling up for Sahil was laundry. Every washing day the basket overflowed and the chair beside it was buried too. At last he saw that he dropped his shirts on the chair each evening, so he dragged the basket right next to it. By Wednesday the chair was bare.

qa.q: What did Shalini dump on her bed?
qa.a: Shalini dumped everything off her floor on the bed.

qa.q: Why did Vishal's tidy-up fail while Sahil's and Shalini's worked?
qa.a: Vishal only hid the clutter, so the mess stayed and his shoes went missing, whereas Sahil split the job into parts and Shalini made one pile to sort into cupboard, shelf and bin.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling as he stood in the middle of his room?
qa.a: Overwhelmed: his chest tightened and he thought the mess was too much.

qa.q: What could Vishal do next Sunday?
qa.a: Vishal could pull everything out from under the bed and sort it into piles, or do one small section at a time.

grounding: Four approaches to cleaning and chores: splitting the job, sorting from one pile, hiding the mess, and fixing the cause when a chore keeps piling up.
